## Decision And Authority

Recommend **OpenTofu with separate Azure and AWS provider implementations**, immutable container images, and versioned application/artifact interfaces. Deploy to Azure first; retain AWS as a migration target, not a simultaneous production commitment. This is a proposed infrastructure convention, not an instruction to provision resources or an approval to change the [committee-reviewed Azure alert sequence](azure-alert-execution-plan.qmd). The [AWS alert alternative](aws-alert-execution-plan.qmd) remains review-only. A change from their proposed Bicep and AWS CDK conventions requires owner approval before implementation.

The [architecture](../explanation/architecture.qmd), [project status](status.qmd), [roadmap](roadmap.qmd), [publication gates](publication-gates.qmd), and applicable ADRs retain authority over ownership, implemented behavior, and approval. This plan adds a deployment and migration view across the whole workspace; it does not authorize publishing, collecting recipients, or sending alerts. Current cloud alert infrastructure, the subscription service, and the V2 producer/consumer runtime are **not implemented** merely because they appear below.

Portability means the same container images, configuration contract, data meaning, release evidence, and operational checks can be reused where their dependencies permit. It does **not** mean that Azure resources, infrastructure state, credentials, databases, queues, or provider-specific application code can be moved to AWS unchanged. Measure and test each adapter, including external Snowflake, Azure Blob, Entra, and provider dependencies.

The [repository map](../agents/repository-map.md#submodule-boundaries) owns source boundaries. The following are deployment proposals, not claims that these workloads are already running on either cloud. Cost keys refer to the explicit scenarios below; they are compute-only unless stated otherwise.

|---|---|---|---|
| Forecast ingestion, transformation, wind and GloFAS (`TC-ECMWF-Forecast-Pipeline`) | Separate scheduled/manual Container Apps Jobs; keep approved Snowflake loading or local outputs | ECS Fargate tasks invoked by EventBridge Scheduler | F: package and measure native geospatial dependencies, scratch space and large upstream downloads; move schedules only after source availability and output equivalence are checked. Snowflake loading is not replaced by container hosting. |

### Entra SSO And Workload Identity

Count registrations by interactive user-facing application and environment, not by container. A browser SSO app registration is distinct from non-interactive workload identity and deployment federation.

| Component | Entra app registration for user SSO? | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Subscription registry | **Yes.** Single-tenant registration and enterprise application per environment. Review production/staging callback URIs; the [AWS alternative](aws-alert-execution-plan.qmd) keeps Entra SSO through application-owned OIDC rather than App Service Easy Auth. | Only currently specified browser SSO client. |
| Dashboard | **Undecided.** If restricted data requires authenticated human access, use a separate registration per environment; do not reuse the registry client by default. | Current dashboard deployment options do not define an SSO boundary; resolve it before exposing the service. |
| Data API | **No, as currently documented.** Data routes use `X-API-Key`; documentation routes are accessible without a key. | Adding Entra SSO would change the upstream API contract and needs an explicit owner decision. |
| Forecast, impact, report jobs, delivery and resolver workers | **No interactive SSO.** Use workload identities and service-to-service authorization. | These components do not sign human users into browser sessions. |
| GitHub Actions / infrastructure deployment | **No user SSO.** Use GitHub OIDC federation to the Azure deployment identity or AWS deployment role. | Keep this non-interactive deployment identity separate from browser SSO clients. |

Container Apps supports finite [manual, scheduled, and event-driven jobs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/jobs); [ECS Scheduler](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/scheduled_tasks.html) starts tasks separately from long-running services. Evaluate [App Service, Container Instances and AKS](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/compare-options) or AWS App Runner, Batch and EKS only against actual networking, CPU/memory, job-duration and operating requirements. Do not adopt Kubernetes solely for portability: it adds cluster and data-service operations without removing provider-specific state and identity.

### Choosing The Azure Web-Service Host

The alternatives in the inventory are candidates, not a decision to support both hosts for every service. At Gate 1, each owner records expected availability, traffic shape, cold-start tolerance, health and rollout needs, private-network/data access, identity, and budget. Pick one **provisional** host for the representative nonproduction test; at Gate 3, run the same image and workload against that host, then approve the host, SKU, minimum replicas, scaling rules, and cost before production IaC is finalized. Reprice the selected configuration; the ACA compute rows below are comparison examples, not a commitment to ACA.

- Prefer **Container Apps** when container-native revisions/traffic management or HTTP/event-driven autoscaling are useful and the workload tolerates scale-to-zero cold starts or has an explicitly priced minimum replica. See Microsoft's [scaling](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/scale-app) and [revisions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/revisions) guidance.
- Prefer **App Service for Containers** when this is a conventional, continuously available web application and its managed web-app lifecycle, including [staging-slot swaps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/app-service/deploy-staging-slots), is a better operational fit than Container Apps scaling/revisions. Confirm the required Linux container, networking, health, and scaling features against the chosen plan.

For the **dashboard**, test its existing nginx/Dash/tile-server image, same-origin routes, Snowflake/Blob access, worker constraint, warm-up, and expected steady/peak traffic. For the **Data API**, test Blob access, request latency, download behavior, and scale-out. A single-instance workaround is acceptable only if it runs one application process/worker and quota resets on process restarts or rollouts are explicitly accepted. It does not enforce a cross-worker, cross-revision, or durable quota. If enforcement must span those events, require shared quota state and contract tests before enabling them; neither hosting choice supplies that state. Neither Azure choice removes Azure-specific dependencies or commits the AWS target to an equivalent managed service.

## Infrastructure And Configuration Convention

| Choice | Benefit | Cost or limitation | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| [OpenTofu](https://opentofu.org/docs/language/providers/requirements/) | Terraform-compatible HCL and provider model for Azure/AWS; open-source project | State, providers and resource semantics remain provider-specific; review provider and backend compatibility | **Preferred**, subject to platform-owner and provider/support review. Pin the CLI, providers and modules; commit the provider lock file. |
| [Terraform](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/providers) | Broad multi-cloud provider ecosystem, modules and reviewed plans | Separate license terms apply to newer releases; remote state is sensitive and provider resources are not portable | Viable if license and support review pass; pin versions and do not mix ownership with OpenTofu over a resource. |
| [Pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/) | Multi-cloud resources in familiar programming languages; managed or self-managed state | Another runtime/SDK and state backend; code can increase review burden | Viable if the team explicitly prefers code and accepts the operating model; do not mix it with OpenTofu over the same resource. |
| [Bicep](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/azure-resource-manager/bicep/overview) | Strong Azure Resource Manager coverage, Azure-native what-if and no separate Bicep state file | Azure-specific; requires a separate AWS IaC convention | Appropriate for Azure-only scope, not as the sole cross-cloud convention. |

OpenTofu's [state](https://opentofu.org/docs/language/state/) maps configuration to real resources; its [backend configuration](https://opentofu.org/docs/language/settings/backends/configuration/) documents remote state and credential precautions. Terraform's [providers](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/providers) have independent versions, and its [backend documentation](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend) likewise warns that state and saved plans can contain sensitive values. OpenTofu and Terraform compatibility is not a promise of automatic state interchange: select one tool for each resource set and rehearse any approved tool migration from a backup.

Containerized applications and reviewed interfaces are the portability unit, not an assertion that IaC state or cloud resources migrate automatically.

### Proposed Layout And Release Process

1. After approval, add a root-owned infrastructure area with **separate environment roots** for Azure and AWS and modules for network, identity, artifact storage, registry, workload execution, observability, and independently gated subscription/delivery resources. This is proposed organization, not an existing `infra/` tree. Keep component code and images in their owning upstream repositories; root coordinates compatible image digests and release manifests.
2. Bootstrap a narrowly scoped state backend separately: private, encrypted, versioned Azure Blob for Azure stacks and S3 for AWS stacks, with tested backend-specific locking, access audit, backup and restore. Separate state by provider, environment and trust boundary. Restrict state and plan access; avoid putting secret values in state, configuration, images, command arguments or logs. Do not point two tools or state files at the same resource.
3. Use separate production and nonproduction accounts/subscriptions where available, region-specific configuration and resource tags for owner, environment and cost. Maintain least-privilege runtime identities separately from deployment identities. Use short-lived CI federation with protected environments, narrowly scoped trust and reviewed permissions; no static cloud keys in GitHub.
4. Build owner-specific OCI images once, pin base images and dependency versions, generate an SBOM and vulnerability evidence, publish immutable digests, and promote the same tested digest across environments and registries. Private Data API checkout requires authorized access; do not expose credentials to fork pull requests.
5. On pull requests, run formatting, validation, provider-aware security/policy checks and credential-free mocked plan tests; review a deployment plan and cost delta. Use OpenTofu validation and plan-only or provider-mocked checks for offline validation; tests that apply infrastructure can create real resources. Never give a pull request arbitrary cloud credentials. Protected deployment jobs apply only approved plans; follow with health, access-denial, artifact-integrity and dependency checks. Schedule drift detection and alert rather than silently applying destructive changes.
6. Configuration is an explicit versioned workload contract: image digest, command, resource limits, region, source/artifact references, schedule and secret **references**, not secret values. Resolve cloud secrets at runtime with least privilege and rotation ownership. Use a separate no-send configuration and IAM/resource policy; a feature flag alone is not evidence of disabled delivery.
7. Record rollback image/configuration and compatible schema versions per deployable. Test restoring state and data, rollbacks, backup retention, resource limits, and incident ownership. Never destroy or replace stateful resources solely because an automated plan proposes it.

## Data, Identity And Cloud Migration

- **Artifacts:** define a versioned storage-reference adapter carrying provider, container/bucket, object key, immutable version and explicit SHA-256. Verify bytes and schema, publish the final manifest last, and retain provenance. S3 ETags are not general-purpose content checksums. Replication must include required object versions and deletion/retention behavior; verify inventories and checksums before switching reads.
- **Data API:** first keep the API's existing Azure Blob read path, with scoped credentials and approved cross-cloud network/egress. To eliminate that dependency, the upstream API owner must implement and verify an S3-compatible storage adapter, catalog and download semantics, source-data migration, and quota behavior. An infrastructure-only change cannot deliver this.
- **Dashboard and producers:** forecast and impact currently use Snowflake for important paths; the dashboard's stage options are local, Azure Blob or Snowflake, not a documented S3 adapter. Inventory SQL, native dependencies, external feeds and secrets; decide whether Snowflake stays or separately approve replacement adapters and verify equivalent outputs. Moving compute does not migrate Snowflake state or contracts.
- **Identity and recipient state:** retain Entra workforce/B2B policy. AWS application-owned OIDC and session validation must replace Azure Easy Auth assumptions; prove session expiry and revocation behavior. Migrate subscription records only after consent, residency, access, encryption, retention and deletion/restore approval; map Cosmos optimistic concurrency to explicitly tested DynamoDB conditions/transactions. Separate source, subscription and operational state.
- **Delivery:** Azure SQL and PostgreSQL schemas/transactions, Service Bus and at-least-once SQS, and provider feedback differ. Rebuild and test inbox/outbox, unique claims, suppression, version checks, ambiguity and reconciliation. Exactly-once provider delivery is not assumed. One active dispatch authority and a fenced routing epoch are mandatory; never dual-send or automatically reactivate a legacy sender on rollback.
- **Cutover:** establish inventory, owners, data classifications, source licensing, region/residency, budgets and recovery objectives first. Build the target separately; copy immutable artifacts and compare independent expected evidence in a **non-sending** shadow. Reconcile checkpoints and historical/retained versions; rehearse restoration and rollback. Only an accountable approval can fence the old writer and promote the new authority. Keep old evidence read-only for its approved retention; retire resources only after reconciliation and rollback windows close.

## Ordered Delivery And Acceptance Gates

1. **Inventory and approvals:** confirm each workload's owner, actual current runtime, region, data classification, external credentials and quotas; obtain platform/tenant access, budget and recovery requirements. Exit with an approved, costed deployment inventory and provisional host assumptions for each web service. Unknown requirements remain blockers, not defaults.
2. **Portable release proof:** agree IaC convention, bootstrap isolated state and CI federation, build the consultation image and provision a nonproduction Azure environment. Run the manual synthetic-only Job; verify pinned digest, SBOM, checksums, private output, repeatability and that Snowflake, recipient, queue and provider access are absent. Azure's existing plan remains the controlling stage-A boundary.
3. **Producers, API and dashboard:** separately package and validate forecast, impact, Data API and dashboard with synthetic/non-sensitive data, measured memory/scratch/duration, explicit Snowflake/Blob network access, health checks and rollback. Use the host-selection criteria above to approve one Azure host, SKU, replica floor and scaling policy for each web service, and reprice that configuration before production IaC. Do not move data ownership or make real data public. Choose schedules only after output parity and operational owners approve.
4. **Non-sending alert shadow and registry:** first implement the separately owned V2/source/consumer runtime and finalized handoff. Then exercise shadow and compare independently sourced evidence under the [Azure plan](azure-alert-execution-plan.qmd); deploy the independently owned registration service according to its [approved sequence](alert-subscription-service-plan.qmd). No send-capable role, credential, route or resource is present. A registry preference is not delivery eligibility.
5. **AWS rehearsal:** after AWS account, policy, region and Entra approvals, reproduce the approved non-sending synthetic deployment using the same digest and separate AWS state; verify storage checksums, IAM denials, dependency connectivity and cost. Implement provider adapters and run source/replay comparisons before considering data or authority migration. The AWS plan's independently staged registration proposal does not reorder the current Azure roadmap without approval.
6. **Delivery and regional expansion:** only after separate privacy, security, source licensing, accessibility, policy, operator, provider and Country Office approvals, implement and test transactional delivery state, resolver, suppression, reconciliation, routing fences and recovery. Authorize a specific controlled cohort before any live send; regional cells and failover need measured SLO/RTO/RPO and residency evidence. No deployment or replay alone authorizes this stage.

For optional local deployments, use synthetic fixtures, local artifact directories and existing container images; a future Compose file may start individual services with fake credentials and explicit non-sending profiles. Local-only execution is useful for development, not a prerequisite for production and not proof of real IAM, Entra, Snowflake, provider, cross-cloud or managed-service behavior.

## Illustrative Costs

All values are **USD per month**, before tax, discounts, support, labor, and unlisted services. They are sizing examples, not quotes, measured utilization, capacity guarantees or total cost of ownership. Azure prices below are East US retail rates retrieved **2026-11-03**; AWS Fargate examples are US East (N. Virginia) Linux/x86 rates from [AWS Fargate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing/). Regions are illustrative, not residency recommendations. Prices and SKU availability must be rechecked for the approved account and region.

### Comparable Compute Examples

Assume a 730-hour month, one Linux/x86 task or replica, **1 vCPU and 2 GiB** unless marked otherwise, and the exact billed hours shown. Azure Container Apps consumption active meters from the [East US retail API](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=serviceName%20eq%20%27Azure%20Container%20Apps%27%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27) are `$0.000024/vCPU-second` plus `$0.000003/GiB-second`, or **$0.108/hour** for that size. The AWS example uses `$0.000011244/vCPU-second` plus `$0.000001235/GiB-second`, or **$0.0493704/hour**. AWS includes image-pull time and a one-minute Linux minimum; Azure jobs bill active execution. Azure idle replicas use different rates; the always-active assumption is deliberately conservative for the selected compute meter. No shared free grants are subtracted, so the Azure figures are gross rather than a predicted invoice. Azure's [consumption terms](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/container-apps/) provide subscription-wide monthly grants and meter requests separately.

These rows are independent scenarios, not a recommended combined deployment. Sizes and durations are unmeasured; forecast/impact may need much larger containers, parallel tasks, scratch space and download time. Do not charge a second tile-server row when it runs in the same dashboard container. Always-on tasks lack multi-zone redundancy; image rebuilds, failed/retried jobs, extra replicas, ingress/load balancing, public IPs, NAT, logs and source reads add cost. The L row omits all state, queue, resolver and provider charges and is **not** a delivery-system estimate.

### Storage, Registry, Subscription And Shared Costs

- **S — Blob/S3 object storage:** 100 GB retained for a month on Azure General Block Blob v2 Hot LRS at the first-tier East US [retail meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=serviceName%20eq%20%27Storage%27%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27%20and%20contains%28skuName%2C%27Hot%20LRS%27%29%20and%20contains%28meterName%2C%27Data%20Stored%27%29) is **$2.08** for storage only; this is a storage-unit scenario for private artifacts or Data API source data, not a measured dataset size. For an AWS reference, the [existing Frankfurt model](aws-alert-execution-plan.qmd#cost-model-frankfurt-pricing-reference) uses S3 Standard **$0.0245/GB-month**, or **$2.45** for 100 GB, retrieved 2026-10-28. These are different regions, not a price comparison; requests, object versions, replication, backup, egress and static hosting are extra.
- **G — image registry:** Azure Basic Container Registry's East US [retail meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=serviceName%20eq%20%27Container%20Registry%27%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27) is `$0.1666/day`, approximately **$5.00 for 30 days**, before any other charges or upgrades. The AWS Frankfurt model uses ECR storage at `$0.10/GB-month`: **$0.50 for 5 GB** before transfer and other costs. Validate included storage, private networking and regional requirements before selecting a tier.
- **U — registration:** Azure's currently recommended App Service is not the Container Apps example above. An East US Linux B1 [retail meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=serviceName%20eq%20%27Azure%20App%20Service%27%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27%20and%20contains%28productName%2C%27Linux%27%29) is `$0.017/hour`, or **$12.41 for 730 hours** for one plan instance. The East US [Cosmos serverless retail meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=serviceName%20eq%20%27Azure%20Cosmos%20DB%27%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27%20and%20productName%20eq%20%27Azure%20Cosmos%20DB%20serverless%27) is `$0.25/million RU`; an illustrative 5 million RU adds **$1.25**, giving **$13.66** of App Service plus request-meter cost before Cosmos storage, network, Entra and other services. B1 may not meet required VNet, availability, authentication or performance features; price the approved tier. The separate Frankfurt AWS evaluation example, including one small Fargate task, ALB, NAT, DynamoDB and stated allowances, is **$91.83/month**; its two-AZ registration example is **$179.31/month**. Different footprints and regions; not a like-for-like comparison.
- **LD — complete future delivery:** the [AWS Frankfurt model](aws-alert-execution-plan.qmd#cost-model-frankfurt-pricing-reference) estimates **$286.56/month** for its controlled-pilot footprint and **$1,137.17/month** for a busier cell; these include its stated database, networking, queue, provider and usage assumptions. Azure's East US [Service Bus Premium retail meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=serviceName%20eq%20%27Service%20Bus%27%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27) is `$0.9275/hour` per Messaging Unit: one unit for 730 hours is **$677.08/month**. The illustrated 0.5-vCPU/1-GiB Azure worker adds **$39.42** of compute, so the known Azure subtotal is **$716.50/month before Azure SQL, resolver, networking, provider, monitoring and recovery**. These different partial footprints are not comparable quotes or approval to send; obtain an exact-region full design estimate after requirements are approved.
- **N — Snowflake:** the existing upstream [cost estimate](https://github.com/unicef-drp/Ahead-of-the-Storm-ORCHESTRATION/blob/main/COST_ESTIMATE.md) states `$3/credit`, `$3/active hour` for an XS warehouse, `$0.18/active hour` for a CPU_X64_XS Snowpark node, and `$1.23/active hour` for CPU_X64_SL; it reports approximately `$0.53–1.26` for measured/inferred legacy pipeline runs under its May 2026 assumptions. These are historical estimates, not current account rates, and must not be added to a cloud total until current Snowflake services, credits and credit price are verified.
- **C — CI/deployment and documentation site:** GitHub's [standard Linux 2-core runner rate](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing) is `$0.006/minute`, so **1,000 billable minutes use $6.00** of compute (each job's partial minute rounds up). The [billing guide](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions) states GitHub Free includes `$12/month` of shared compute usage; the example adds `$0` only while that allowance remains. Standard runner use for public repositories and GitHub Pages workflows is free. The actual organization plan, repository visibility, usage and Pages storage/traffic are unknown, so no GitHub Pages hosting invoice is estimated. Azure Storage static website and S3/CloudFront remain migration alternatives; price their requests, DNS/TLS and bandwidth separately.
- **X — shared costs:** Illustrative East US Azure meters total **$73.53/month** for one Azure Container Apps environment private-endpoint meter at `$0.10/hour` for 730 hours (**$73.00**), 1 GB of Basic Logs ingestion at `$0.50/GB` (**$0.50**), and 10,000 Key Vault Standard operations at `$0.03/10K` (**$0.03**); see the [Container Apps meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20serviceName%20eq%20%27Azure%20Container%20Apps%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27%20and%20meterName%20eq%20%27Environment%20Private%20Endpoint%27), [Azure Monitor meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20serviceName%20eq%20%27Azure%20Monitor%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27%20and%20meterName%20eq%20%27Basic%20Logs%20Data%20Ingestion%27), and [Key Vault meter](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?%24filter=armRegionName%20eq%20%27eastus%27%20and%20serviceName%20eq%20%27Key%20Vault%27%20and%20priceType%20eq%20%27Consumption%27%20and%20skuName%20eq%20%27Standard%27%20and%20meterName%20eq%20%27Operations%27). This omits NAT, egress, SQL, retention, state, backup and other endpoints. The AWS Frankfurt reference totals **$54.81/month** for one NAT gateway at 730 hours (**$37.96**) plus 1 GB processed (**$0.052**), one interface endpoint in one AZ at 730 hours (**$8.76**) plus 1 GB (**$0.01**), 10 GB CloudWatch logs ingested and retained for a month (**$6.624**), one Secrets Manager secret (**$0.40**) and one KMS key (**$1.00**), using rates in the [Frankfurt cost model](aws-alert-execution-plan.qmd#cost-model-frankfurt-pricing-reference). This single-AZ example is not a production-availability design; the regions and footprints differ, not a like-for-like comparison. Price actual NAT, DNS, IPv4, log retention, backup, storage, egress and endpoint counts after topology and retention are approved. ECMWF licensing, Entra, support and engineering depend on contract and use; no combined monthly total is defensible without those inputs.

Before approving spend, measure representative job duration, CPU, memory, scratch, storage/version retention, requests, logs and egress; price the same availability and region assumptions in both [Azure Pricing Calculator](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/calculator/) and [AWS Pricing Calculator](https://calculator.aws/). Include each environment, realistic redundancy, shared-cost allocation and contingency. Reconcile actual bills against budgets and keep a named owner for each unpriced dependency.

## Changes Needed In Existing Plans

Do not edit the existing plans as part of this proposal. If the portable convention is approved, their owners should review and update them together:

- **Azure alert execution:** replace or explicitly reconcile the proposed Bicep/shared-release-plane convention with the selected OpenTofu modules and state ownership; preserve the reviewed stage order, workload boundaries, no-send controls, source authority, fencing and regional gates. Add approved Azure workload and shared-resource cost inputs.
- **AWS alert execution:** reconcile the proposed CDK/CloudFormation convention with the selected OpenTofu modules, bootstrap, identities and separate state; retain its AWS-specific auth, persistence, queue, provider, security and recovery requirements. Reconcile registration/shadow sequencing with the Azure roadmap rather than silently changing it. Refresh the Frankfurt model when account, region and workload are known.
- **Subscription service:** document the approved portable identity/session and storage interfaces and their Azure/AWS implementations, without treating Easy Auth, Cosmos and DynamoDB as equivalent. Preserve independent ownership, no-send behavior and PII controls.
- **Roadmap and architecture:** only after decisions and implementation are approved, record the selected convention, actual component ownership, adapter readiness and any changed sequencing. Do not present this proposed plan as a shipped cloud platform or a new publication/send authorization.
